doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: His daughter Tracy and his other children's musical talent
summary: His daughter Tracy became a self-taught bassist, and his other children showed early talent.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: Well Tracy has had a pretty good run—

Yeah. She has. She started playing late. She studied dance. She studied at Martha Graham and at ABT and then she went to SUNY up in Brockport as a dance major. She got discouraged, I think her physical appearance discouraged her and she dropped out and came back to New York and met a young musician who I had worked with a couple of times and they became close and he bought her a bass and she bought herself a Rubank book and just—

In six months she was working. In two years she was working with Phyllis Hyman. Yeah she’s done really well. They showed musical talent — my middle daughter, when she was four, could sing any note I could hit on the piano. I’d try to play the most unlikely, the oddest intervals, F to B, octave low to B flat or to A or whatever. And I’d say, “Sing it honey” and she was four years old. The keyboard came up to here on her and she’d sing it clear as a bell. Any interval I could think. I’d just hit intervals at random, the oddest intervals. And I knew right then, man a four year old kid who can do that, she’s got a great sense of relative pitch. And my older son, Jimmy, he’d play on the table or on the chair with his fingers, absent mindedly, along with something on the radio or a record of mine. And he used to astound me, the things he thought of at eight years old. He kind of used to browbeat me because I thought he could pick up some things, rhythmic figures and accompaniment, that I couldn’t think of. He could play complicated six-eight rhythms in the third grade. So to me it was obvious that the two of them were really talented. But Tracy, my oldest one, it wasn’t so obvious to me. Dancing I could see at a young age that she was well coordinated and she could hear the beat and so forth. But it
wasn’t until she started playing that she just astounded me. To me she really is a great player, one of my favorite bass players. And I don’t say that because she’s my daughter.
Do you get to work together?

We have a couple of times but not much. She’s graceful, she’s both imaginative and practical, she’s meticulous, devoted to anything that she perceives as being of importance. You add that up and you’ve got a good studio musician.
